title: Monitoring & reporting financial performance
blurb: Monitor actual and committed costs against the time-phased budget, and choose the right financial report for each audience and decision.
question: A school extension project shows actual costs £25k below the budget for month four, and the project manager is about to report it as under budget. The finance officer points out that £40k of orders were placed this week. How should the project manager monitor and report the project's financial position, and which reports would the sponsor expect?

teach.body: Financial monitoring means regularly comparing actual and committed costs with the time-phased budget, analysing the variances and forecasting the final cost. Financial reporting passes that picture to the people who need it, in a form they can act on. Plain English: where has the money gone, what have we promised to spend, where are we heading, and does anyone need to decide something? Reports that don't lead to decisions are just paperwork.

teach.caption: The forecast (estimate at completion, or forecast to complete) matters as much as the spend to date.

teach.body: ACTUAL costs have been incurred: invoiced, paid or booked. COMMITTED costs have been promised, through orders placed or contracts signed, but not yet invoiced. Once money is committed it can't be spent on anything else, so a report that shows only actuals makes the budget look healthier than it is. The true headroom is the budget minus actual AND committed costs.

teach.caption: Reporting actuals alone would have told the sponsor good news that wasn't true.
Forecast against budget, with an illustrative ±5% tolerance. Inside it, the PM corrects and reports routinely; a forecast outside it goes to the sponsor in an exception report.

teach.text: Exam trap: an underspend is not automatically good news. Spending below plan may mean work is late, invoices haven't arrived or orders haven't been committed yet. And actual cost below planned value does not prove the work is under budget: that needs earned value.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Explain monitoring: compare actual and committed costs with the time-phased budget each period.
Explain that variances are analysed for cause, and the final cost is forecast (EAC).
Name two or three report types and what each is used for (variance, cash-flow, earned value, exception, dashboard).
Link to governance: within tolerance the PM acts; beyond it, escalate to the sponsor.
Monitor actual AND committed costs against the time-phased budget.
Analyse variances for cause and forecast the outturn every period.
Different reports answer different questions: variance, cash flow, earned value, forecast, contingency, commitments, exceptions.
Tailor the detail to the audience: summary and decisions for the sponsor, detail for the PM.

summary: You can now explain how a project manager monitors actual and committed costs against the time-phased budget, analyses variances and forecasts the final cost. You can also match each type of financial report to its purpose and audience, and explain when a variance must be escalated.

A.q: Which report would show the sponsor every purchase order and contract placed but not yet invoiced?
A.why: A commitment report lists money already promised through orders and contracts, showing the true headroom left in the budget.

whyNot.0: A cash-flow report shows when money will move, not the list of commitments.
whyNot.2: A lessons learned report records experience to pass on, not financial commitments.
whyNot.3: An earned value report compares PV, EV and AC; it doesn't list orders placed.

A.q: A sponsor asks for a report that compares planned and actual spend for each cost line and explains the differences. Which report is this?
A.why: A cost or variance report sets budget against actual for each line and explains the variances.

whyNot.0: A contingency drawdown report covers only the contingency used and remaining.
whyNot.1: The risk register records risks and responses, not planned versus actual spend.
whyNot.3: A benefits profile shows when benefits are expected, not spend.

A.q: The board wants to see how much of the risk contingency has been used so far, on which risks, and how much is left. Which report fits BEST?
A.why: A contingency drawdown report shows each release of contingency against the risk that triggered it and the balance remaining, showing that risk spending is controlled.

whyNot.0: A cumulative spend-to-date report shows total spend to date, without linking it to risks.
whyNot.1: A commitment report covers orders and contracts placed, not contingency.
whyNot.2: A cash-flow forecast shows the timing of future payments.

B.q: Actual costs are £20k below budget to date, but a £35k equipment order was placed yesterday. Which statement is correct?
options: The order only counts once paid
The order should go in contingency
B.why: Committed costs reduce the available budget as soon as the order is placed. Including the £35k commitment, the project is £15k over its budget to date.

whyNot.0: This ignores the commitment, overstating the headroom.
whyNot.1: Waiting for payment hides money already promised, which is why commitments are tracked.
whyNot.2: Contingency is for identified risks; a planned purchase is a commitment against the budget.

B.q: When is an exception report MOST appropriate?
options: At the end of every reporting month
When the project is formally closed
When a supplier sends an invoice
B.why: An exception report escalates a forecast breach of agreed tolerances to the sponsor or board, with causes and options for a decision.

whyNot.0: Routine monthly reporting uses progress, cost and variance reports.
whyNot.2: Closure uses the final financial report and closure report.
whyNot.3: Individual invoices are processed routinely and recorded as actual costs.

B.q: The finance director needs to know how much money the project will need in each of the next six months. Which report should the PM provide?
B.why: A cash-flow forecast shows when money will be needed, so finance can make funds available at the right time.

whyNot.1: A variance report looks back at budget against actual, not forward month by month.
whyNot.2: An exception report escalates a tolerance breach.
whyNot.3: A dashboard summarises key measures; it doesn't set out monthly funding needs.

C.q: For three months, actual spend on a project has been well below the planned spend. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Report it as a saving to the sponsor
Release the surplus back to finance
Find out why spend is below plan
Spend the surplus on extra features
C.why: An underspend can mean delayed work, late invoices or uncommitted orders rather than a real saving. The PM must understand the cause before reporting or acting on it.

whyNot.0: Calling it a saving before knowing the cause could mislead the sponsor.
whyNot.1: Funds shouldn't be released until it's clear the work won't still need them.
whyNot.3: Extra features are a scope change needing change control, and the 'surplus' may not be real.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of regular financial reporting?
options: Giving early warning of budget issues
Supporting timely decisions by the sponsor
Showing how contingency is being used
C.why: Reporting informs decisions; it never replaces change control. Scope changes must be assessed and approved through the change process.

whyNot.0: Early warning is a core purpose of regular reporting.
whyNot.1: Reporting exists to support decisions at the right level.
whyNot.2: Contingency drawdown reporting shows risk spending is controlled.

C.q: An iterative project has a stable team, so its cost per two-week time box hardly changes. What financial information is MOST useful to its steering group?
options: Spend per time box against value delivered
A monthly variance on every single invoice
A forecast of when the S-curve will flatten
A list of each team member's daily hours
C.why: With cost fixed per time box, the useful question is what each time box buys: spend against features or value delivered, and how much scope the remaining budget will cover.

whyNot.1: Invoice-level variance detail is for the PM and finance, and adds little where cost is a steady run-rate.
whyNot.2: With a steady run-rate, the spend line is almost straight, so this tells the group little.
whyNot.3: Daily hours are operational detail, not information for a steering group.

reteach.title: Your bank account and the credit card
reteach.question: Your bank app says you have £800 left this month. But you've booked a £300 holiday deposit on a credit card that hasn't been billed yet. How much can you really spend?

blocks.h: Spent, promised and what's really left
blocks.body: The bank balance shows money actually gone (actual costs). The credit card booking is money you've promised but not yet paid (a commitment). Your real headroom is £500, not £800. A sensible household also looks ahead: when are the big bills due (cash flow)? And if something pushes you well past your limit, you'd tell your partner before it happens rather than after (an exception report).

blocks.text: Looking only at what has been paid is like trusting the bank balance and forgetting the card bill. Always count commitments.

explain.body: Monitoring compares costs with what the time-phased budget says should have been spent BY NOW, not with the total budget. That shows whether spending is running ahead of or behind the plan at this point.

test.q: At month four, what should actual and committed costs be compared with?
test.why: The time-phased budget gives the amount planned to be spent by month four, which is the fair comparison at that point.

whyNot.0: Comparing with the total budget can't show whether spending is on track at this point.
whyNot.2: Other projects' costs may help estimating but aren't this project's baseline.
whyNot.3: A price list helps estimate, not monitor against the plan.

explain.body: A commitment arises when an order is placed or a contract signed. It reduces the budget available immediately, even though the invoice comes later. Tracking it avoids double-spending the same money.

test.q: A £50k contract is signed today; the supplier will invoice in three months. When does it first reduce the budget available to the PM?
test.why: Signing the contract commits the money, so it reduces the available budget straight away.

whyNot.0: Waiting for payment would let the same money be promised twice.
whyNot.1: Acceptance is later; the money was committed at signing.
whyNot.3: Closure is far too late to account for a signed contract.

explain.h: Pick the report for the question
explain.body: Each report answers one question: variance (how far from plan?), cash flow (when is money needed?), earned value (cost and schedule together), forecast (where will we end up?), contingency (how much risk money is left?), exception (what needs a decision?).

test.q: The sponsor wants a single page with red, amber and green ratings for cost, schedule and risk. Which format fits?
test.why: A dashboard gives a quick, visual summary of key measures, often with RAG ratings, suited to senior audiences.

whyNot.0: A commitment report lists orders and contracts placed.
whyNot.1: A cash-flow forecast shows the timing of money needed.
whyNot.2: A final account settles a contract at the end.

explain.body: The sponsor and board need the forecast, exceptions and decisions required. The PM needs full variance detail. Work package leads need their own budgets. Tolerances decide what is escalated: within them the PM acts; beyond them the sponsor decides.

test.q: What should a financial report for the project board focus on?
options: The detailed cost of each task
test.why: Boards need a summary: where the project is heading, any breaches of tolerance and the decisions they must make.

whyNot.1: Invoice-level detail is for the PM and finance, not the board.
whyNot.2: Personal expenses are an administrative matter, not board information.
whyNot.3: Task-level detail belongs at work package and PM level.
